'''Clayton Howell Heathcock''' (born July 21, 1936) is an American organic chemist, professor emeritus of chemistry, and former dean of the College of Chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name="cv">{{cite web |title=Curriculum Vitae |first=Clayton H. |last=Heathcock |publisher=Department of Chemistry, University of California, Berkeley |url=https://heathcock.org/chhgrp/chhcv.pdf |format=PDF |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref> He is known for total syntheses of complex polycyclic natural products and was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1995<ref name="nas">{{cite web |title=Member Directory |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |url=https://www.nasonline.org/membership/member-directory/page/102/}}</ref> and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1991.<ref name="aaas">{{cite web |title=Member Directory |publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/directory?page=229}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Heathcock graduated from Brackenridge High School in San Antonio in 1954, earned a B.S. in chemistry from Abilene Christian College in 1958, and received a Ph.D. in organic chemistry from the [[University of Colorado Boulder]] in 1963 under [[Alfred Hassner]]. He completed a postdoctoral fellowship with [[Gilbert Stork]] at [[Columbia University]] (1963–1964).<ref name="cv"/>

== Academic career ==
He joined the UC Berkeley faculty in 1964, rising to full professor by 1975. He chaired the Department of Chemistry (1986–1989) and was named dean of the College of Chemistry in 1999, succeeding [[Alexis T. Bell]].<ref name="dean1999">{{cite web |title=Organic Chemist Clayton H. Heathcock Named Dean... |publisher=UC Berkeley Public Affairs |date=August 12, 1999 |url=https://newsarchive.berkeley.edu/news/media/releases/99legacy/8-12-1999.html}}</ref> He held the Gilbert Newton Lewis Professorship (2003–2005) and served as chief scientist of the California Institute for Quantitative Biosciences (QB3) from 2005 until his retirement in 2008. He also chaired the Organic Chemistry Division of the [[American Chemical Society]] and was editor-in-chief of ''[[Organic Syntheses]]'' and the ''[[Journal of Organic Chemistry]]''.<ref name="cv"/><ref name="faculty">{{cite web |title=Clayton H. Heathcock |work=Faculty Profile |publisher=College of Chemistry, UC Berkeley |url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/people/clayton-heathcock}}</ref>

== Research ==
Heathcock's research focused on total synthesis of complex polycyclic natural products, including the Daphniphyllum alkaloids, altohyrtin, and the spongistatins, and on new stereoselective methods, with particular attention to the [[aldol reaction|aldol condensation]]. In 1977 and 1978 he and students Charles Buse and William Kleschick demonstrated that by using preformed lithium enolates the stereochemical outcome of the addition to aldehydes can be predicted using a mechanistic rationale for the reaction that was first introduced by [[Howard Zimmerman]] and Margaret Traxler, the so-called Zimmerman–Traxler Transition State. This established the aldol addition reaction as a general method for stereocontrolled synthesis.<ref name="jorgchem1980">{{cite journal |last1=Heathcock |first1=C. H. |last2=Buse |first2=C. T. |last3=Kleschick |first3=W. A. |last4=Pirrung |first4=M. C. |last5=Sohn |first5=J. E. |last6=Lampe |first6=J. |title=The Aldol Condensation of Preformed Enolates |journal=Journal of Organic Chemistry |year=1980 |volume=45 |pages=1066–1081 |doi=10.1021/jo01294a030}}</ref> In all, Heathcock published roughly 285 papers.<ref name="cv"/><ref name="berkeleynews2019">{{cite web |title=College of Chemistry to Build New Heathcock Hall with Gift of $25 Million |work=Berkeley News |date=October 16, 2019 |url=https://news.berkeley.edu/2019/10/16/college-of-chemistry-to-build-new-heathcock-hall-with-gift-of-25-million}}</ref> With [[Andrew Streitwieser]], he coauthored the textbook ''Introduction to Organic Chemistry'' (1976), which eventually appeared in three subsequent editions and was translated into multiple languages other than English.<ref name="bnf">{{cite web |title=Authority Record |publisher=Bibliothèque nationale de France |url=https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb12281652k}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
His honors include the Ernest Guenther Award (ACS, 1986), the ACS Award for Creative Work in Synthetic Organic Chemistry (1990), the Prelog Medal (ETH Zurich, 1991), election to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1991),<ref name="aaas"/> election to the National Academy of Sciences (1995),<ref name="nas"/> the Centenary Medal of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (1996), the Herbert C. Brown Award for Creative Research in Synthetic Methods (2002),<ref name="berkeleyan2002">{{cite web |title=Awards |work=Berkeleyan |date=February 27, 2002 |url=https://newsarchive.berkeley.edu/news/berkeleyan/2002/02/27_award.html}}</ref> and the Paul Gassman Award for Distinguished Service (2004).<ref name="cv"/>

== Heathcock Hall ==
In October 2019, UC Berkeley alumnus Terry Rosen, a former doctoral student of Heathcock's, and his wife, Tori, donated $25 million toward a new College of Chemistry building to be named Heathcock Hall in his honor.<ref name="berkeleynews2019"/> Ground was broken in summer 2024 on the four-story facility.<ref name="capital">{{cite web |title=Heathcock Hall Capital Campaign Update |publisher=College of Chemistry, UC Berkeley |url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/heathcock-hall}}</ref> In 2025, Heathcock was interviewed for UC Berkeley's Emeriti Legacy Project.<ref name="emeriti">{{cite web |title=Clayton Heathcock, Professor Emeritus, Chemistry |work=Emeriti Legacy Project |publisher=UC Berkeley Retirement Center |url=https://retirement.berkeley.edu/clayton-heathcock-professor-emeritus-chemistry}}</ref>
